In her tent in central Gaza early one morning last month, 31-year-old Fida al-Toutah, a mother of five, was combing her daughter's hair when the sound of gunfire erupted.
"My mother shouted at us to get down," her son Ezz recalled, weeping as he spoke.
He only realised Fida had been hit when he saw the bloodied hands of his younger brother, who had been clinging onto his mother as the bullets came in.
"Our mother was so kind and generous. What did she do wrong?" Ezz said.
Fida died on 21 September from a gunshot wound to the head.
She is among more than 1,400 people in Gaza who have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war - which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
On the ground in Gaza, it meant that Israel's large-scale bombardment stopped, which brought substantial relief and an increase in humanitarian aid and medical supplies entering the territory.
But even during the ceasefire, Israel has continued launching strikes in Gaza almost every day. In the past week alone more than 30 people have been killed, according to Gaza's health ministry.
Israel says it is targeting Hamas operatives, and accuses Hamas of continued violations of the ceasefire.
"It [the ceasefire] is all lies. Every day there's a shooting. Every day there is killing and death lurking around," said Ahed, Fida's husband.
In response to the BBC's questions about Fida's killing, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they had no record of the incident.
The total death toll from Israeli attacks since the start of the war in Gaza three years ago now stands at more than 74,000, according to the Gaza health ministry.
Outside Fida's tent, her brother Ibrahim pointed to the holes he said were made by a volley of bullets fired by Israeli forces.
"This tent is just a piece of cloth. Imagine that a military vehicle came down here and fired a spray of bullets," he said. "There was also gunfire coming from the sky, from above, from quadcopters, and it was directed at unarmed civilians."
Fida is the fourth of Ibrahim's siblings to be killed since the start of the war. "We left our neighbourhood Zeitoun to survive, but death is following us," he said.
The family has moved seven times but safety has been out of reach. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million population has been displaced multiple times by the war, the UN says, with many forced to live in tented cities and unsafe structures.
On the same day that Fida was killed, 14-year-old Ismail al-Bardawil was also shot dead. He was killed in the al-Mawasi area of Rafah, in southern Gaza.
His family told the BBC that he was shot by Israeli forces while he and his brothers were fishing in the Mediterranean Sea, around 20m (66ft) from the shore. He is one of more than 300 children killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to Gaza's health ministry.
The IDF said it had no information about this incident either.
Over the past year, the IDF has released videos of its operations in Gaza targeted at Hamas and other groups. At least seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since the start of the ceasefire.
Both Fida and Ismail lived close to the so-called Yellow Line that separates the areas occupied by the Israeli military in Gaza from areas controlled by Hamas in the west.
Areas around the line are considered the most dangerous because Israeli forces have frequently opened fire there. But there are few options to move because there is an extreme shortage of space.
The strip was densely populated even before the war began. Now, its population is squeezed into under 40% of its area, which is controlled by Hamas.
In those areas the group maintains a tight grip, clamping down on dissent and still recruiting fighters.
In May this year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had directed the IDF to increase the area of Gaza under Israel's control to 70%.
Architect Amal Alabadla, who lived in a comfortable flat prior to the war, now lives in a tent on the coastline.
"Every time the rains come, it gets flooded. I feel very scared when the wind is strong because our tent gets destroyed or damaged," she said.
Amal is forced to raise her two boys - Mohammed and Noah - on her own.
Her husband was not in Gaza when the war broke out, and in three years they have not been reunited. Amal's three brothers, who helped her care for the boys, were killed in separate attacks before the ceasefire began.
"During the winter, my son suffers from epilepsy seizures because of the cold. It's very hard sometimes to keep him dry and warm," she said.
"Before the war, I had a job, a house, an ordinary life, but then everything turned upside down. Now we have no hope, nothing. It's only about survival day by day, to keep my kids alive, clean, healthy and fed."
There are camps further inland in Gaza that have even been built below sea level, which are at greater risk of flooding.
The October 2025 peace deal was supposed to pave the way for the reconstruction in Gaza, but rebuilding has not yet begun - stuck in limbo because of an impasse over the second phase of the deal.
Israel strictly controls what materials and machinery are allowed into Gaza, acting, it says, for reasons of its own security.
Earlier this year, US President Donald Trump put forward a plan to disarm Hamas, but in August it was rejected by Netanyahu, who stated that no military pull-out would happen until Hamas was "genuinely" disarmed.
Hamas has said handing over its heavy weapons is contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.
Half a world away, Trump's Board of Peace has also proposed a recovery plan for Gaza worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn).
But, one year on from the ceasefire and three years on from the start of the war, many like Amal are deeply sceptical of things actually changing on the ground.
"We are struggling and not being allowed to rebuild," she said. "I don't think they are telling us the truth about allowing us to rebuild a safe future for our children."
Additional reporting by Imogen Anderson and Malak Hassouneh

articles.full_text:
No agreement in sight between Russia and Ukraine, the United States and Russia are certain. “The war in Ukraine could lead to further escalation and the spread of the conflict beyond the country’s borders,” said US Secretary of State Rubio. “There is currently no prospect of resolving the conflict in Ukraine through negotiations,” US Secretary of State Rubio concluded. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov echoed this sentiment: “There is currently no path to a peaceful solution in Ukraine.”
Meanwhile, US-Russian economic and financial negotiations continue. Senior Russian and US officials have held talks to involve an American investor in the Nord Stream gas pipeline project, Reuters reports . The discussion participants included Jared Kushner – businessman and son-in-law of the US President – and Kirill Dmitriev, special representative of the Russian President.
The United Kingdom has also extended sanctions against Russia and expanded its sanctions list against Russia by 26 items. On the European front, Kiev’s performance remains disappointing. “We must stop giving Kiev false hope about joining the European Union,” wrote European Rapporteur . “No one seriously assessing the situation believes that Ukraine will become an EU member by the end of the decade, if it ever does. There are more effective ways to help Ukraine: for example, admitting the country to NATO and providing military aid,” a European official commented. At the same time, EU diplomats believe that splitting the accession negotiations for Ukraine and Moldova is only a matter of time. Meanwhile, Hungary has lifted its veto on the technical phase of the EU accession negotiations for Ukraine and Moldova, the Rapporteur portal reported , citing sources. The next step will be to agree on draft common positions; if approved, these could pave the way for the opening of two sets of accession negotiating chapters.
“Moldova is establishing ‘protective zones’ at border crossings with Ukraine in anticipation of possible drone attacks,” Newsmaker reports . “Border guards, civil servants, and citizens at checkpoints will be able to evacuate to safety.”
Tensions between Russia and NATO are also rising. “NATO could block Russia’s access to the Baltic Sea within hours in the event of an attack on one of the Alliance’s member states,” Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said. “This would create an existential crisis for Moscow.” The minister noted that approximately 60% of Russian seaborne oil exports pass through the Baltic Sea, as do the routes used by ships bound for Kaliningrad. At the same time, Tsahkna acknowledged that there are currently no signs of preparations for a Russian attack. The Lithuanian army will guard the border with the Kaliningrad region for two weeks, with the possibility of extending the period, Interior Minister Martynas Katelinas stated.
Danish intelligence reported that “Russia has begun conducting sabotage operations against Danish companies supplying equipment to Ukraine, after concluding that its larger-scale sabotage attempts had failed to reduce military support for Kiev.” “In the spring, we saw a lot of planning but very little execution. In early summer, however, we saw the launch of many more operations,” said Josefine Christiansen, a senior analyst with the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, speaking at a national security conference in Copenhagen. According to the official, Russia concluded that its previous strategy, targeting a wide range of targets, “failed to dissuade the West and NATO from supporting Ukraine.”
South Korea has recalled its ambassador from Ukraine; the decision was announced by Seoul following Kiev’s statements regarding the dispatch of two North Korean soldiers captured by the Ukrainian army to a war zone. Kiev is said to have violated confidentiality rules.
Unlike the United States and Russia, Ukraine has expressed its readiness for various ceasefire solutions, according to Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Tykhyi. Specifically, this includes an unconditional and comprehensive ceasefire. The possibility of a truce in the Black Sea, brokered by Turkey and Egypt, is also being considered. Furthermore, discussions are underway regarding an energy ceasefire and a food truce brokered by India, as well as an energy truce brokered by the United States. The only remaining issue, it appears, is the Russian Federation’s readiness. Moscow has repeatedly stated that it is not interested in a temporary ceasefire.
Internet data indicates a decline in internet connection quality in some neighborhoods of Kiev, following a series of Russian drone strikes targeting energy infrastructure, causing emergency power outages. The Borshchahivka chemical-pharmaceutical plant in Kiev, one of Ukraine’s largest pharmaceutical companies, was attacked.
Kiev’s air defense system shot down a Geran-5 attack drone using a MANPADS system near the SBU Academy. Emergency power outages were implemented in the Chernihiv, Sumy, and Poltava regions, according to regional energy companies.
The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office has sent requests to the Ministry of Justice and Security of the Netherlands, as well as to other countries, for the arrest and extradition of nine representatives of the International Criminal Court (ICC) who were convicted in absentia in the Russian Federation. The individuals in question are ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan, Court President Piotr Józef Hofmański, First Vice-President Luz del Carmen Ibáñez Carranza, and Judges Tomoko Akane, Rosario Salvatore Aitala, Sergio Gerardo Ugalde Godínez, Bertram Schmitt, Reine Alapini-Gansou, and Haikele Ben Mahfoudh.
Kiev responded to the data center attack by attacking Russian data centers: A fire broke out at a Yandex data center in the town of Sasovo, Ryazan region, following a drone (UAV) attack. Yandex shares fell more than 3% following a drone attack on a data center in the Ryazan region. CIAN reported a service outage following an attack on the Yandex data center.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov made several statements at his morning press conference regarding the Russia-Ukraine-Iran situation: “The oil fire on the tanker in the Black Sea did not cause environmental problems; ‘we got away with it’; Russia is convinced that a solution in Ukraine must be comprehensive; partial measures will not be enough; Agreements on Ukraine must be guaranteed and last ‘for generations’; Russia appreciates India’s interest in the issue of a solution in Ukraine; If Iran truly intends to withdraw from the NPT (Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty), the topic could be addressed during the meeting between Putin and Pezeshkian; the CIS (Commonwealth of Independent States) format has proven its value and relevance, serving as a basis for more advanced forms of integration.”
And now a look at the frontline updated at 3:30 PM on October 8. Russian forces continued their attacks on Ukrainian territory. During the night, Ukrainian sources reported explosions in the Kyiv region, near Hlevah and on the outskirts of the capital. Monitoring sources reported a UAV attack on a power substation near Vyshhorod. In the Odessa region, attacks on facilities near Izmail were reported.
Overnight, Ukrainian forces claimed responsibility for the attack on the Yandex DC LLC data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Region. In Bashkortostan, facilities belonging to Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat were also hit.
In the Chernihiv region, Russian aviation and Geran drone crews struck UAV assembly and storage plants near Chernihiv, Semenivka, and Pekurivka, as well as a border detachment of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine (SBGS).
Fighting continues in the direction of Sumy. OSINT sources report Russian advances in Kyyanytsya and Khotin. Small-arms firefights are ongoing in the wooded area of Shostka District. Ukrainian forces are strengthening reserve defense lines and redeploying their reserves.
One dead in a drone attack in the Kursk region.
In the Belgorod region, two people were injured by agricultural assaults. Administrative buildings and residential buildings were damaged.
Fighting is ongoing in the Kharkiv sector. Russians have attacked Ukrainian positions near Velykyi Burluk, Chornohlazivka, Myshchenky, Prykolotne, Novoselivka, Kupyne, Derhachi, Novyi Burluk, Varvarivka, and Ternove. In Dergachi, a temporary deployment point for Colombian mercenaries of the Ukrainian National Guard was destroyed. Fighting continues near Tokarivka, in the Lyptsi sector.
In Donetsk, three civilians were injured in Horlivka following drone (UAV) attacks.
In Luhansk, drone strikes killed one person and injured six others.
Clashes continue in the Lyman sector. Ukrainian forces are launching counterattacks in the Yampil and Zarichne areas.
In the Kupyansk sector, fighting continues near Kupyansk-Vuzlovyi and in the northern part of Kupyansk. Ukrainian forces are attacking railway infrastructure in Kupyansk-Vuzlovyi. The main fighting is focused on specific positions and supply lines along the Oskil River.
In the Druzhkivka district, fighting is ongoing near Oleksijevo-Druzhkivka. In Dobropillya, Russian units are conducting offensive operations in the southern, central, and northern districts of the city.
In the Zaporizhia sector, the Russians are continuing offensive operations after capturing Holubkove and Samoylovka. Fighting continues in the Orikhiv direction for the city of Orikhiv, which has been targeted by Russian air forces. Repeated attacks have been reported on bridge infrastructure in Zaporizhia, which is crucial to enemy military logistics in the area.
In the Kherson district, Ukrainian forces continue to attack with FPV drones and remotely mine roads in the Oleshky district. Two people have been killed in Ukrainian attacks. Russian artillery and UAV crews continue to pound AFU positions on the right bank of the Dnieper River.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, during a visit to Lisbon, Portugal, said that Washington's pressure on NATO allies to increase defense spending “is not a hostile act.” He stressed that stronger member states make the Alliance itself, allied ties and deterrence against threats stronger, PBS NewsHour reports.
Rubio was in Portugal as part of a trip to NATO countries that also included Iceland and Greece. He acknowledged that smaller states, including Portugal, may find it difficult to secure funds for major military projects. At the same time, he said that every Alliance country must be as strong as possible.
Portugal's defense spending
According to NATO data, Portugal, with a population of fewer than 11 million people, spends slightly more than 2% of its gross domestic product on defense. The country's government says it intends to raise this figure to about 3%, including through investments in dual-use civilian infrastructure.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Rubio praised Lisbon's steps toward meeting NATO's target. At the same time, the planned level of spending remains below the 5% of GDP demanded by U.S. President Donald Trump. The American president has repeatedly criticized allies for insufficient defense spending and for shifting what he believes is a disproportionate burden onto the United States.
Statements on Russia's war against Ukraine
Rubio also warned about the risk of the consequences of the war that the Russian Federation, an aggressor state, has been waging against Ukraine since the full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, spreading further. In his view, a likely stalemate in the war could trigger military escalation in Europe, including a campaign of sabotage in neighboring NATO states. European officials have accused Moscow of sabotage and destabilizing actions aimed at undermining support for Ukraine.
The U.S. secretary of state said that the Trump administration would continue trying to facilitate a negotiated settlement of the war, but called the process difficult. He added that Washington would not invest in processes that do not make progress possible. As the outlet reported, the statement came after new Russian strikes in eastern Ukraine that killed 30 people.

articles.title: Rubio says U.S. pressure on NATO allies to boost defense spending is 'not hostile' - PBS
articles.summary: Rubio says U.S. pressure on NATO allies to boost defense spending is 'not hostile'  PBS
articles.full_text:
LISBON, Portugal (AP) — U.S. pressure on NATO allies to increase their defense spending "is not a hostile thing," U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Thursday, but reiterated that the Trump administration wants the military alliance to be a stronger deterrent against threats.
Rubio told reporters during a visit to European NATO ally Portugal that "the stronger the members of NATO are, the stronger NATO is, the stronger the alliances and the stronger the deterrence is."
President Donald Trump has long railed against NATO allies for spending too small a fraction of their national budgets on defense, leaving the United States to shoulder what he says is an unfair burden. Some members of the 32-country alliance have been reluctant to divert funds from other government policies, however.
"People sometimes view this call to invest more in defense as a hostile thing," Rubio said. "It is not a hostile thing."
Rubio, who was in Portugal on the last leg of a three-nation tour of NATO allies that also included Iceland and Greece, acknowledged that some smaller NATO members, such as Portugal, have difficulty finding the funds for major military projects.
"Every country is of a different size and proportion. Some countries can contribute more than others, but every country in NATO needs to be as strong as they can possibly be," Rubio told a news conference in Lisbon.
He noted the danger of the war in Ukraine, following Russia's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022, spilling beyond Ukrainian borders. An apparent stalemate in Ukraine could bring a military escalation in Europe, he said.
"That escalation could wind up being a sabotage campaign in neighboring countries that are members of NATO," he said. That could "quickly turn what is a war between two countries into a much broader and far more dangerous regional conflict."
European officials have accused Moscow of a campaign of sabotage and disruption aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations.
Rubio also said that the Trump administration will keep trying to facilitate a negotiated settlement to the war, but that it has been difficult.
"We have tried, we will continue to try, but we're also not going to invest in pointless processes if we can't make progress," he said, coming after new Russian strikes in eastern Ukraine killed 30 people.
Meanwhile, Rubio also praised Portuguese efforts toward meeting the NATO target for defense spending.
Portugal, a country of fewer than 11 million people, spends just over 2% of its gross domestic product on defense, according to NATO. The government says it plans to increase defense spending to around 3%, including dual-use investments in civilian infrastructure.
That still leaves it below the 5% of GDP set aside for defense spending that Trump has demanded and that requires investment at an unprecedented scale in Europe.
Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel said at the news conference that his country views its relationship with the U.S. as "fundamental."
Portugal provided support for American operations in the Iran war by allowing the U.S. to use the Lajes Field air base in the mid-Atlantic Azores islands, which is strategically located for military refueling flights.
The U.S. Air Force has long had a base there under an agreement with Portugal. Unlike neighboring Spain, where Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, a Socialist, refused to allow the American military to use Spanish bases to stage operations for attacks on Iran, Portugal's center-right government granted Washington "conditional approval" to use Lajes Field.
"Portugal is a great ally, very cooperative ally of the United States and a country with which we already have a solid and growing relationship. And we visit these countries in order to reinforce those ties," Rubio said before arriving in Lisbon. "That's the purpose of the trip."
Some Portuguese political parties balked at the decision to allow the U.S. to use the Azores islands air base, however. Following a formal complaint by a small left-wing political party called Left Bloc, the country's attorney general's office said last week that it's looking into whether the use of the Lajes Field base was lawful.
Rubio visited Portugal a day after delivering a speech in the Greek capital, Athens, urging European countries to save Western civilization by upholding the values and traditions of ancient Greece.

articles.title: Bulgaria blames war in Ukraine for less security in Black Sea - The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
articles.summary: Bulgaria blames war in Ukraine for less security in Black Sea  The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
articles.full_text:
SOFIA, Bulgaria -- Bulgaria's president said Wednesday that Russia's war in Ukraine has led to "a significant deterioration" in security in the Black Sea region.
President Iliana Yotova spoke to reporters after an emergency meeting of the country's Security Council following drone attacks on ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast. While she didn't directly blame Russia for those strikes because there's an ongoing investigation by Bulgarian authorities, Yotova said the war in Ukraine was undermining security for commercial vessels.
"Russia's war against Ukraine has led to a significant deterioration of the security environment in the Black Sea region," she said. "There is a growing trend of attacks by maritime and aerial drones against commercial vessels, leading to damage and the sinking of ships, as well as loss of life."
Senior government and security officials discussed the Balkan country's maritime security and critical infrastructure in the context of the war in Ukraine.
"The Security Council categorically condemns the attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea as a gross violation of international law and demands a fast check to identify the perpetrators," Yotova said.
On Tuesday, two commercial vessels were struck by drones in the first attack on shipping in the NATO member's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
Sea and aerial drones attacked the two ships about 80 miles off Bulgaria's coast.
The Togo-flagged ship Alfa Watan suffered critical structural damage and sank at the scene. The second vessel, the Palau-flagged Able, caught fire after the attack. A Bulgarian ferry evacuated all 18 crew members.
Bulgarian maritime authorities said Wednesday that the search efforts for the crew of Alfa Watan had been suspended and wouldn't resume.
Vice Admiral Rumen Nikolov, who led the rescue operation, said no survivors or bodies had been found. He said the drone strike had sparked an extremely powerful explosion, and the ship had sunk almost instantly.
Bulgarian authorities said the origin of the drones was under investigation, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for the drone strikes.
In a statement sent to local media on Wednesday, the Russian Embassy in Sofia rejected Russian involvement in the drone attacks on the two ships, saying "they were not among the targets hit by Russian armed forces."
It quoted the Defense Ministry in Moscow as saying that "to determine the 'nationality' of the drones used to strike the ships, it is necessary to wait for the results of the investigation."
Tuesday's attacks came a day after a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank in the Black Sea. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued.
While Bulgaria and Romania are still narrowing down the list of suspects, the European Commission confirmed on Wednesday that they had asked for satellite imagery following the attacks, and that the European Union, which has a center that analyzes data from space, is providing them.
Should the accusations made by Zelenskyy prove true, the attacks conducted on a NATO member's territory would mark a new escalation in what European leaders and intelligence officials have said is a growing hybrid campaign by Russia aimed at testing the military alliance and the 27-nation EU.
Hybrid attacks can aim to destabilize a country, probe its defenses, strain resources, or influence public opinion -- often in a way that makes it hard to identify those responsible.
An Associated Press interactive map tracking the incidents of hybrid attacks shows an escalation, from 59 in March 2025 to more than 200 at this point.

articles.full_text:
Yemeni government forces have said they “neutralised” 1,860 Houthi fighters since launching a large-scale counteroffensive to retake territory under the control of the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God.
The spokesperson for the internationally recognised government’s military said in a social media post early on Thursday it had carried out 2,103 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi military positions across several fronts as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” campaign.
The Yemeni government, backed by Saudi Arabia, also says its forces have captured strategic mountain positions in western Taiz overlooking the coast.
Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, announced on Sunday the Dawn of Yemen operation to retake all Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group has controlled since 2014.
Battles in Yemen have focused in recent days on areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the US-Israel war on Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
Forces aligned with the Yemeni government launched an operation on Tuesday to recapture strategic territory near the strait and around the city of Mocha, which the Houthis had taken last month.
Coalition targeting
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said on Wednesday it destroyed 82 Houthi military targets in the Yemeni governorates of Saada, Hodeidah, al-Jawf and Marib.
The spokesperson for the coalition said in a statement that the targets included missile sites, including “11 mountain-based ballistic missile storages in Saada, command and control centres, communication systems, missile and weapons storages”.
The latest operation followed Houthi attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday targeting King Khalid international airport in Riyadh and Abha international airport, according to the spokesperson.
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said the attacks on the two airports killed three people.
One person was killed and eight were wounded in an attack on King Khalid airport, while two people were killed and 28 were wounded in the attack on facilities at Abha airport, the GACA said in a statement.
The attacks have drawn condemnation from across the region. Kuwait denounced the attacks as a “flagrant violation” of Saudi sovereignty and international law. Egypt said the attacks threaten the security of the entire region.
The Mecca-based nongovernmental organisation Muslim World League also condemned the strikes, describing them as “treacherous terrorist attacks”.
As the fighting rages on, Yemen’s permanent representative to the United Nations, Abdullah al-Saadi, met the UN secretary-general’s special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, on Wednesday to discuss the situation in the country.
During their talks, al-Saadi accused the Houthis of rejecting peace initiatives and de-escalation efforts proposed by the Yemeni government.
He stressed that the government’s goal is to extend its control across the entirety of the country and end the Houthis’ ability to wage war. He said the government is seeking a permanent end to the war and is not interested in a temporary truce, arguing that such a scenario would only lead to fighting later.

articles.title: EU agrees to sanction over 1,600 people and entities linked to Russia's war - Euronews.com
articles.summary: EU agrees to sanction over 1,600 people and entities linked to Russia's war  Euronews.comEU envoys approve new Russia sanctions listings, diplomats say  ReutersEU Approves Record Sanctions Expansion Targeting 1.6K Russian Citizens and Entities  The Moscow TimesRussian supplier dropped from EU sanctions package at Estonia's request  ERREU extends Russia sanctions over hybrid attacks and destabilization abroad for another year  Ukrinform
articles.full_text:
The EU will soon add over 1,600 names, including 77 lawmakers who stood for election in the occupied territories of Ukraine, to its Russia sanctions. The decision comes amid an unsettling rise in hybrid attacks.
The European Union has agreed the single largest expansion of its sanctions list against Russia, adding 1,646 names in one go.
The deal, sealed on Wednesday by ambassadors in Brussels, covers 743 individuals and 826 entities accused of supporting Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Separately, it targets 77 lawmakers who stood in the Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine for the widely discredited State Duma election in September.
Ambassadors wrapped up the agreement after several weeks of deliberations and legal scrubbing, which was particularly intensive given the sheer number of names.
It will be formally approved on Monday when foreign ministers gather in Luxembourg. The targeted people and entities will then be made public.
Sanctions entail a travel ban, an asset freeze and a prohibition on providing funding.
Member states were keen to close the agreement to portray a united front amid a rapid succession of hybrid attacks, some attributed to Russia. Work has already begun on new listings in response to the drone incident at the Leipzig airport in Germany.
Another reason to project unity is last month's contentious decision to remove two high-profile oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, from the blacklist.
Usmanov's removal, at France's request, was tied to a prisoner release with Azerbaijan brokered by the Turkic states, which have long lobbied in the billionaire's favour. One French citizen has been released while a second remains in prison.
In exchange for the painful concession, the EU extended the sanctions list for an unprecedented three years. In total, the blacklist will soon cover almost 4,650 names.
Earlier this week, High Representative Kaja Kallas celebrated the three-year renewal but admitted it is unlikely that Usmanov and Fridman will be included again.
"Countries are free to put forward names that should be included in the sanctions list. But in the end, it is up to the member states to decide," Kallas said.
"And I do not see this on these two persons happening any time soon."
Brussels is still grappling with the aftermath of the Usmanov saga and the precedent it might have set for the common foreign policy, which relies on unanimity.
As the bloc prepares to admit new members, the European Commission has proposed using the so-called passerelle clause to move from unanimity to qualified majority voting on issues such as sanctions, thereby avoiding the multiplication of vetoes.
But the clause creates a textbook Catch-22: it requires unanimity to end unanimity.

articles.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to Kagan and Soai - BBC
articles.summary: Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded to Kagan and Soai  BBCNobel chemistry prize goes to pair who solved mystery of 'mirror image' molecules  ReutersA molecule’s ‘handedness’ can determine whether it’s an effective drug – 4 examples of pharmaceuticals where chirality matters  The ConversationNobel Prize in Chemistry Is Awarded to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai  The New York TimesA Nobel for illuminating life’s asymmetry  The Economist
articles.full_text:
Chemistry Nobel awarded for solving mystery of life's asymmetry
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry has been awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai for providing a solution to the chemical mystery of life's asymmetry.
The researchers discovered how nature exclusively makes the correct version of a molecule - rather than its mirror image.
For example, amino acid molecules, the building blocks of proteins, exist as two forms that are each other's mirror image.
But living organisms on Earth only function with one of those forms. The Nobel laureates answered the question: why does life favour just one of these mirror image molecules over the other.
In organic chemistry, this property is known as "chirality", so chiral molecules have both right and left-handed forms.
You can think of them as looking like our hands - not identical, but each a mirror image of the other.
And while nature almost exclusively produces the version it requires to function, chemical reactions in a lab usually create a 50-50 mix of both left- and right-handed molecules.
When it comes to making drugs, this is particularly significant, because each version behaves differently when it interacts with our bodies.
So, one might have disease-fighting properties, while the other version does nothing or even causes harm.
The development of the Thalidomide drug is an example of this. In the 1950s it was prescribed to pregnant women suffering with morning sickness. But it is a chiral molecule - the right-handed version is an effective treatment, but the left-hand is toxic.
The original drug given was a mixture of the two, and it was later discovered that the body will convert between the two. The result was thousands of children, born to women who took the drug, developed severe disabilities.
Speaking to the Nobel Prize press conference this morning over the phone, Kenso Soai said: "This is one of the most exciting days of my life."
By solving the mystery of chirality, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai worked out how to design chemical reactions to produce much more of the desired version of a molecule.
Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, explained: "Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality - the selective production of the correct version of a molecule - can emerge spontaneously.
"The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."
Henri Kagan, who is at Université Paris-Sud, first discovered a new way of manipulating chemical reactions in 1986. This allowed him to create a greater excess of one of the mirror images than had previously been thought possible.
Kenso Soai from Tokyo University of Science took the next step in 1995. He published a scientific paper in the journal Nature describing the first ever chemical reaction that had the potential to be homochiral - producing only the desired version of an organic molecule.
In 2003, he finally succeeded in controlling a reaction in which only one of the two possible mirror images was formed.
"Other than life itself," the Nobel Committee said in a statement, "no one had previously achieved this feat".
At the press conference on Wednesday, Kenso Soai praised the "many, many excellent researchers" in this field.
Professor Robert Mokaya, president of the UK's Royal Society of Chemistry said it was a "powerful example of how fundamental chemistry can underpin solutions to some of the biggest challenges facing society".
"Different isomers (or versions of molecules) can have completely different biological and physical effects, so they are crucial in finding effective medicines to treat all sorts of illnesses," he added.
Prof Angus Davison, from the University of Nottingham, studies the biology of chirality and said that the Nobel-winning chemistry could help reveal how and why life favours "one-handedness".
"In ways that we don't yet quite understand, the chirality of the basic building blocks of life ends up making bodies that are themselves also chiral," he told BBC News.
This was the foundation, he explained, of our hearts being on left hand side of our bodies and snail shells that coil to the right.
Peter Somfai, a member of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said the research awarded this year's prize has become part of "our basic understanding of how chemistry functions".
He said showing how a mirror image is created is "probably the most fundamental question in life - because somehow that happened four billion years ago when life was created. And now we have, for the first time, mimicked that in the lab".

articles.title: Russian Spies Give 'MatchBoil' Malware a Stealthy Facelift - Dark Reading
articles.summary: Russian Spies Give 'MatchBoil' Malware a Stealthy Facelift  Dark Reading
articles.full_text:
Cyber-espionage actor UAC-0099 has been steadily refining its flagship dropper in campaigns targeting Ukrainian organizations.
A likely Russia-affiliated cyber-espionage group is using an increasingly sophisticated malware downloader to target Ukrainian organizations across the transportation, manufacturing, and energy sectors.
According to ESET, the group, tracked as UAC-0099, is using the downloader, dubbed MatchBoil, to deliver MatchWok, a C# backdoor that gives the attacker persistent access to compromised systems.
The security vendor's analysis showed that MatchBoil has been in active development since at least 2024, and has kept steadily improving with every iteration since then. Though its core function remains the same — to download additional payloads — the latest edition of the malware features stronger obfuscation, sandbox checks, and evolving persistence mechanisms, researchers warn.
A Constantly Evolving Malware Strain
Overall, MatchBoil has evolved from what ESET terms a "one-shot downloader" into a dropper capable of repeatedly retrieving updated payloads from its command-and-control (C2) server.
"Our investigation of MatchBoil samples from April 2024 to April 2026 revealed multiple modifications, from code-level structure to the use of the .NET Reactor obfuscator, all of these implemented in a relatively short time," ESET said in a technical report this week. "This demonstrates a keen interest by UAC-0099 operators in improving their downloader, not only to avoid detection by security solutions, but also to use it as a key part of their toolset in future attacks."
Russia-Aligned Cyber Espionage?
UAC-0099 is a threat actor operating since 2023, which ESET believes with moderate confidence is linked to Russian interests, primarily because it targets Ukrainian organizations. The security vendor also thinks it's likely that UAC-0099 is an initial access broker for Sandworm, the threat actor linked to Russia's military intelligence agency and responsible for numerous destructive attacks on Ukraine's power grid and other infrastructure. In the MatchBoil campaign, UAC-0099 initially targeted transportation companies before expanding its focus to manufacturing and, more recently, the energy sector.
The threat actor's attacks typically have begun with spear-phishing emails containing a link to an archive file with a VBScript payload. Users tricked into downloading and manually executing the script end up with MatchBoil on their systems. Once running, the malware checks for the presence of a specific directory on the victim's machine and terminates if the directory already exists, according to ESET. The malware then obtains specific details about the machine, which it uses to identify the victim during subsequent C2 communications.
MatchBoil: New & Improved Malware Capabilities
Samples of the malware that ESET examined showed UAC-0099 steadily refining MatchBoil to make it harder for defenders to detect and analyze. While the 2024 versions, for instance, relied on relatively basic Unicode-based obfuscation, the 2026 edition uses Eziriz .NET Reactor, a commercial .NET obfuscation and protection tool for making an application's code harder to reverse engineer and analyze. Similarly, newer versions of the malware include sandbox checks and a less conspicuous interface designed to avoid detection by security researchers and users.
UAC-0099 has also been constantly tinkering with MatchBoil's persistence mechanisms, too, ESET noted. Initial versions of the malware used both a registry value and a scheduled task to maintain persistence on compromised systems and ensure the payload would continue to run on them, even through system reboots. Later versions switched to the Windows Run key exclusively to launch the malware when a user logged in to the system. Last year, the malware authors went back to using scheduled tasks as a persistence mechanism.
ESET found that by late 2025, MatchBoil had evolved from a dropper that essentially ran once, contacted its C2 server, and downloaded and installed a next-stage payload, into one that executed every two minutes. The change allowed it to repeatedly contact its control server and retrieve new or updated payloads.
"From all the samples of the downloader that we collected, we see that UAC‑0099 is continually improving MatchBoil for future attacks," ESET concluded. "The samples compiled or seen before November 2025 were much more straightforward and simple to analyze compared to newer ones."

articles.title: US-Israel-Iran War Latest Live News: ‘Enrichment is an Inseparable Part…’ – Iran Rejects US Pressure to Give Up Uranium Enrichment, Eslami Says Tehran Will Not Hand Over Nuclear Stockpiles - The Sunday Guardian
articles.summary: US-Israel-Iran War Latest Live News: ‘Enrichment is an Inseparable Part…’ – Iran Rejects US Pressure to Give Up Uranium Enrichment, Eslami Says Tehran Will Not Hand Over Nuclear Stockpiles  The Sunday Guardian
articles.full_text:
As Washington pushes Tehran to make concrete concessions on its nuclear programme, Iran is drawing a firm line around uranium enrichment. Mohammad Aslami, head of Iran's Atomic Energy Organisation, has said Tehran will neither abandon its enrichment rights nor surrender its uranium stockpiles, keeping the nuclear dispute at the centre of efforts to end the US-Iran war.
Eslami made the remarks in Tehran as the United States demanded a significant reduction in Iran's enrichment capacity. US Vice President JD Vance has said a "meaningful" cut in enrichment will be necessary for Washington to accept a deal aimed at ending the conflict.
The latest exchange highlights one of the biggest obstacles facing diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran: the future of Iran's uranium enrichment programme and its existing stockpile.
Eslami rejected the possibility of Iran stopping enrichment, arguing that the activity forms a basic part of the country's nuclear industry.
“Once again, the issue of uranium enrichment has been raised, and it has been said that it should be put on the agenda for negotiations. But enrichment is an inseparable part of the nuclear process,” Eslami said.
He also accused the United States of applying a double standard to nuclear technology and pointed to Washington's own emphasis on nuclear capabilities.
“Even the Americans have made nuclear technology a priority in their national development, national security, and national defence documents … So these claims are deception and lies.”
Eslami said Iran would continue developing nuclear technology as part of its broader scientific and technological progress.
“Absolutely not. Enrichment is an integral part of the nuclear process. How can you claim to have a nuclear industry without possessing the starting point of this process?”
He also stressed that Iran would not retreat from its position.
“We will not step back,” he added.
Washington has made Iran's enrichment programme a central issue in negotiations over ending the war.
US Vice President JD Vance said Iran must make a “meaningful” reduction in its enrichment capacity before the United States can accept an agreement. He has also questioned why Tehran would need uranium enriched to 60% if it does not intend to develop a nuclear weapon.
The US position goes beyond seeking assurances about Iran's future nuclear activities. Washington wants Tehran to take concrete steps to reduce its enrichment capability and address its stockpile of highly enriched uranium.
That demand directly clashes with Tehran's insistence that it has a right to maintain enrichment as part of its nuclear programme.
The dispute dates back to the 2015 nuclear agreement, formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA).
Under the deal, Iran agreed to limit uranium enrichment to 3.67% and accept restrictions and monitoring on its nuclear activities. The United States withdrew from the agreement in 2018 under then-President Donald Trump and restored sanctions on Tehran.
Iran subsequently moved beyond the limits set by the agreement and eventually enriched uranium to 60%, far above the JCPOA's ceiling. Before the later military strikes, Iran had accumulated a substantial quantity of highly enriched uranium, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency assessments cited by Reuters.
The current status of some of Iran's nuclear stockpile and enrichment infrastructure remains difficult to establish because access for international inspectors has been restricted following the attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has previously indicated that Tehran could discuss limits on its nuclear activities but would not accept a US demand for “zero enrichment.”
Iran has maintained that enrichment represents a sovereign right under the framework of international nuclear agreements, while the United States has focused on preventing Tehran from retaining the capability to produce weapons-grade material.
The two positions leave little room for compromise on the central nuclear question.
The enrichment dispute comes as Washington and Tehran continue efforts to find a way out of the conflict.
Iranian officials have been reviewing US positions through diplomatic channels, with mediators involved in efforts to keep negotiations moving. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Thursday that Tehran was examining Washington's response to its latest proposal and expected to respond within days.
At the same time, the nuclear issue remains closely connected to broader questions involving sanctions, Iran's uranium stockpile and the future of the Strait of Hormuz.
For now, Eslami's comments show that Tehran is not prepared to make the kind of sweeping enrichment concessions Washington has demanded. That leaves uranium enrichment as one of the most difficult issues facing the two sides as they seek a diplomatic path to end the war.

LONDON — Police who searched the properties of the former Prince Andrew and seized his property in the investigation into his links to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein have agreed the search warrants were unlawful, a London judge said Thursday.
Justice Nicholas Hilliard said that the Thames Valley Police had made a significant error in applying for the warrant when they searched the properties of the former prince now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor.
Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on Feb. 19 on suspicion of misconduct in public office and police searched two of his homes. His lawyers asked the High Court judge to invalidate the warrants under which those searches were conducted.
Hilliard said the parties had agreed to invalidate the warrants before the hearing Thursday.
Mountbatten-Windsor was not in court for the hearing.
Stephens, of the Howard Kennedy firm in London, described the hearing as a preliminary skirmish in the broader legal battle.
“It’s the first step of Prince Andrew and his lawyers saying, ‘Actually, this is tainted evidence. It was obtained inappropriately,’” Stephens said. “Therefore it should be excluded from any criminal trial.”
King Charles III stripped Mountbatten-Windsor of his princely title last year as he sought to shield the rest of the royal family from the continuing fallout from his younger brother’s links to Epstein.
While Mountbatten-Windsor, 66, continues to receive a stipend from the king’s private funds, Buckingham Palace has made it clear that those funds may not be used to fund his effort to challenge the search warrants.
The police investigation initially focused on allegations that Mountbatten-Windsor shared sensitive information with Epstein when the former prince was a U.K. trade envoy, but police later said they could also consider other matters.
Police questioned Mountbatten-Windsor for 11 hours before releasing him under investigation, meaning he was neither charged nor exonerated.
It was the first time in nearly four centuries that a senior British royal was placed under arrest.
The allegations against Mountbatten-Windsor came to light when the U.S. Justice Department released millions of pages of documents from its investigation into sex trafficking by Epstein and his connections to a network of wealthy, powerful men around the world.
Mountbatten-Windsor’s ties to Epstein have been a source of embarrassment to the royal family for more than a decade.
Lawmakers questioned the relationship as far back as 2011, when the then-prince was forced to give up his globetrotting role as the U.K.’s special trade envoy. Eight years later, he failed to explain his continuing ties to Epstein in a disastrous interview with the BBC, ending his career as a working member of the royal family.

The United Nations warned on Thursday that El Nino will intensify before peaking in December, bringing higher temperatures to much of the planet and compounding the effects of man-made climate change. The World Meteorological Organization added that this naturally occurring weather phenomenon could be the strongest since at least 1950.
El Nino will intensify even more before peaking in December, the United Nations said Thursday, warning it could be among the strongest witnessed since at least 1950.
The naturally occurring weather phenomenon is set to bring higher temperatures to much of the planet, the UN's weather and climate agency said, with its impact compounding the effects of man-made climate change.
Read moreRare train of cyclones fuelled by historic El Nino make their way across Pacific
"El Nino will continue to intensify ahead of its forecast peak in December," the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in its monthly Global Seasonal Climate Update.
"It is likely to bring above-average temperatures to much of the globe and shift rainfall patterns, increasing the risk of drought and floods in different regions."
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Nino and its opposite La Nina, with neutral conditions in between.
El Nino 'strengthening rapidly'
"Sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are forecast to increase to record levels during October-November-December 2026, reflecting the strengthening of the El Nino event which will drive weather patterns and impact economies, ecosystems and communities across the globe," the WMO said.
The forecast is based on consensus across 13 leading national and international meteorological centres.
"El Nino is firmly established and strengthening rapidly," said WMO chief Celeste Saulo.
"WMO forecasts indicate a near-100 percent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027, potentially being one of the strongest since at least 1950."
Saulo explained that El Nino does not add new heat to the planet, but releases heat being stored in the ocean.
"The ocean it's drawing from is the warmest we've ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release," she said.

articles.title: Iran's Nuclear Deception and 24 Years of Warnings the West Chose to Ignore - Townhall
articles.summary: Iran's Nuclear Deception and 24 Years of Warnings the West Chose to Ignore  Townhall
articles.full_text:
For more than two decades, the world has been warned that Iran’s nuclear program was about far more than a benign pursuit of civilian energy. Yet successive Western governments repeatedly chose negotiation over verification, promises over dismantlement, and hope over evidence. Today, after the United States and Israel have inflicted serious damage on Iran’s nuclear infrastructure and Washington is demanding a meaningful reduction in Tehran’s enrichment capacity, the same fundamental question confronts the West. Will it finally insist on deeds rather than words?
The warning bells rang loudly in August 2002. The National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI) publicly revealed the existence of two secret nuclear facilities in Iran, the uranium enrichment complex at Natanz and the heavy water facility at Arak. The information had reportedly been obtained through networks inside Iran. The revelations shattered Tehran’s claim that its nuclear activities were fully transparent and peaceful. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) subsequently visited the facilities. That disclosure was a watershed moment. It demonstrated that the international community was not discovering Iran’s nuclear activities through its own inspection machinery. It was being alerted by the Iranian opposition.
The history that followed should have taught the West a lesson about the dangers of diplomatic complacency. By 2003, the IAEA was already raising concerns about shortcomings in Iran’s declarations and limitations in the safeguards system. European governments negotiated temporary suspensions. Tehran signed agreements, offered assurances, and later resumed enrichment. The IAEA repeatedly demanded greater transparency, access to facilities and implementation of the Additional Protocol. Yet Iran continued to exploit the gap between political promises and the technical reality of its nuclear program.
The pattern became depressingly familiar. Concealment was followed by exposure. Exposure was followed by negotiations. Negotiations produced partial concessions. Those concessions were followed by renewed construction and another round of diplomacy. Barack Obama’s deeply flawed 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) was presented as the great diplomatic solution. The agreement imposed significant restrictions on Iran’s nuclear activities and created an elaborate system of international verification. But it did not resolve the fundamental strategic question.
Should the Islamic Republic be allowed to retain an industrial-scale enrichment capability that could ultimately provide the infrastructure for a nuclear weapons option? When the United States withdrew from the JCPOA in 2018, the diplomatic architecture began to unravel. Tehran progressively breached the nuclear restrictions imposed by the agreement. By 2021, Iran was enriching uranium to 60 percent, near weapons-grade. That was far beyond the level normally required for civilian nuclear power. The IAEA recorded the progression from enrichment to 5 percent, then 20 percent, and finally 60 percent. This is where the role of the IAEA becomes crucial and painfully limited. The agency has performed an indispensable service by documenting Iran’s nuclear activities. But inspectors cannot verify what they cannot see.
By 2025, the IAEA reported that Iran had removed monitoring equipment and that the agency had lost continuity of knowledge concerning centrifuges, rotors, bellows, heavy water, and uranium inventories. It also warned about Iran’s growing stockpile of highly enriched uranium. By June 2025, the IAEA estimated that Iran possessed 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched up to 60 percent U-235. The agency also stressed that it was unable to verify the whereabouts and status of all such material following subsequent military attacks.
The military campaign has now changed the equation. Israeli attacks in June 2025 struck Natanz and Isfahan. The United States subsequently attacked Natanz, Isfahan, and Fordow. Further U.S. and Israeli attacks hit Natanz again in 2026. Reuters reported in January that Iran’s principal enrichment facilities had been severely affected. The pilot plant at Natanz was destroyed, while underground facilities at Natanz and Fordow were heavily damaged. Yet IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi warned that Iran could eventually resume limited enrichment. That is the crucial point. Bombing centrifuges is not the same as eliminating nuclear capability. Iran possesses scientific expertise, engineers, uranium stocks, and centrifuge technology. It also has a political determination to preserve what it describes as its right to enrich uranium.
The physical destruction of buildings may set the program back, perhaps substantially. It cannot by itself erase the scientific knowledge and technical expertise required to rebuild it. That is why JD Vance’s latest warning deserves serious attention. In a Reuters interview, the vice president argued that Washington cannot simply exchange Iranian assurances for American concessions. If Tehran genuinely has no intention of producing a nuclear weapon, he argued, it should demonstrate that commitment through a meaningful reduction in its enrichment capacity. That is the right principle. Iran’s current position suggests that the regime still wants to preserve the option to enrich. Tehran has reportedly rejected demands to halt enrichment or transfer enriched uranium abroad while continuing to insist that its nuclear program is peaceful. After 24 years of deception, delay, and diplomatic maneuvering, the burden of proof must now rest squarely on Tehran. The West should demand three things. First, Iran must provide full access to the IAEA. Second, there must be a verified accounting of every gram of enriched uranium and every centrifuge. Third, Iran must accept verifiable dismantlement of infrastructure capable of producing weapons-grade material. Anything less risks recreating the very cycle that brought us to this point.
The lesson of Natanz is not that diplomacy failed. The lesson is that diplomacy without credible verification and meaningful consequences failed. The NCRI sounded the alarm in 2002. The IAEA documented the warning signs. Western governments negotiated repeatedly. Iran repeatedly used the resulting breathing space to advance its nuclear capabilities. Now the nuclear facilities may lie damaged, but the nuclear ambition has not necessarily disappeared. The time for another carefully worded Iranian promise has passed. If Tehran genuinely wants peace, it must accept the only currency that can now command international confidence. Verifiable action.

articles.summary: U.S. Makes F-35 Push As Portugal Weighs F-16 Replacement  TWZPortugal seriously considers US F-35 jets along with other options  ReutersMarco Rubio calls Portugal 'ideal gateway' to Europe for US during Lisbon visit  Euronews.comRubio says US pressure on NATO allies to boost defense spending is ‘not hostile’  AP NewsRubio visits Portugal, praising a 'great ally' and looking to build deeper ties  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.full_text:
The United States is stepping up its campaign to sell Portugal the F-35. Speaking in Lisbon today, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the United States would make Portugal a “very competitive” offer to replace its F-16 fleet. The development adds a high-level political push to an increasingly intense competition over the Portuguese Air Force’s next fighter.
Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel said after meeting Rubio that Lisbon is seriously considering the American proposal, while emphasizing that other options remain under consideration.
“The Portuguese state will always decide in accordance with the national interest,” Rangel said at a news conference after the meeting. “There is one point that is also clear: we are seriously considering the F-35 proposal, just as we are considering others.”
Portugal currently operates 25 modernized F-16AM/BMs, including 21 single-seat F-16AMs and four two-seat F-16BMs, from Monte Real Air Base, or BA5. The Portuguese Air Force, known as the Força Aérea Portuguesa (FAP), has not yet formally launched a replacement competition, but the aging fleet is increasingly becoming the focus of attention in Lisbon.
Portugal acquired a total of 45 F-16A/B Block 15 aircraft through the Peace Atlantis I and II programs.
The first 20 aircraft were delivered beginning in 1994. These were new-build F-16A/B Block 15OCU aircraft, comprising 17 single-seat F-16As and three two-seat F-16Bs, and were used to equip Esquadra 201 “Falcões.”
A second batch followed in 1999, when Portugal received 25 former U.S. Air Force Block 15OCU aircraft. Twenty-one were F-16As and four were F-16Bs, with several intended as attrition replacements or spares. These aircraft had accumulated roughly 3,000 flight hours and underwent an extensive modernization program to bring them to the F-16AM/BM configuration. This means the aircraft are broadly comparable to the U.S. Air Force’s F-16C/D Block 50/52 fleet.
Esquadra 301 “Jaguares” finally became operational with its upgraded aircraft in 2005, while Esquadra 201 did not receive its upgraded F-16s until 2011.
Since then, the Portuguese Vipers have continued to receive incremental improvements. Their configuration has progressed through several mission-software standards, while the aircraft have been equipped with night-vision goggles, Joint Helmet-Mounted Cueing Systems (JHMCS), and advanced targeting and weapons capabilities.
Among the more important additions are Northrop Grumman Litening II targeting pods, and the ability to employ weapons including GBU-12 Paveway II laser-guided bombs, GBU-31 Joint Direct Attack Munitions (JDAM), and GBU-49 Enhanced Paveway II dual-mode weapons.
Twelve former Portuguese F-16s were transferred to Romania under a deal signed in 2013, with deliveries taking place in 2016 and 2017. Romania subsequently ordered five additional aircraft in 2019.
Structurally, the Portuguese F-16s could potentially remain in service into the mid-2040s. But maintaining their relevance against increasingly sophisticated air forces would require continued investment in avionics, sensors, communications, and self-protection systems.
The F-16AM/BM fleet continues to rely on the old AN/APG-66(V)2 pulse-Doppler radar. Replacing it with an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar such as Northrop Grumman’s APG-83 would substantially improve detection and tracking performance, but would come at considerable cost.
Portugal faces a choice between continuing to invest in increasingly tired fourth-generation airframes or moving directly into the fifth generation.
Since the end of the Cold War, Portugal has become much more engaged in out-of-area operations and missions in support of NATO.
In the process, the Portuguese F-16 fleet has accumulated an impressive operational record.
The fighters have repeatedly deployed on NATO air-policing missions, including rotations to the Baltic States, Iceland, Romania, and Poland.
The F-35A would give Portugal a fifth-generation fighter built around low observability, sensor fusion, advanced electronic warfare, and networked operations.
The aircraft would also fit naturally into a NATO environment in which an increasing number of European air forces are adopting the F-35.
More than 900 F-35s are already in service or on order across Europe, according to previous comments by U.S. Ambassador to Portugal John Arrigo. Washington has repeatedly argued that joining that community would provide Portugal with a substantial interoperability advantage.
However, European competition includes the Eurofighter Typhoon, Dassault Rafale, and Saab Gripen E, with Airbus preparing an especially aggressive campaign for the Typhoon.
Airbus has said it intends to submit an unsolicited Eurofighter proposal to Portugal in late October or early November. That package is expected to encompass not just the aircraft, but financing, industrial participation and broader military cooperation.
Selecting the American stealth fighter deepens Lisbon’s military relationship with Washington at a time when European governments are wrestling with fundamental questions about their dependence on U.S. military capabilities.
Across the continent, uncertainty over Washington’s stance on NATO is encouraging European allies to examine ways of reducing their reliance on American military technology, even as those same countries continue to increase defense spending and purchase U.S. equipment.
If Washington can combine the F-35’s capability advantages with an attractive acquisition and sustainment package, Portugal could find itself facing a difficult choice between the strategic benefits of joining Europe’s growing F-35 fleet and the industrial and political advantages of selecting a European fighter.
The final decision on the replacement of the F-16 will also determine what combat jet spearheads the Portuguese Air Force for the next several decades.
